19458.title: Artificial Neuron
19458.heading: Artificial Neuron
19458.content:
An artificial neuron computes a weighted combination of its inputs, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function. The output becomes an input to units in the next layer.

Although loosely inspired by biology, the artificial neuron is a mathematical building block. Its weights are learned through procedures such as [[Backpropagation]] rather than specified as symbolic rules.

More precisely, each input is multiplied by a [[Neural Network Weight]], the products form a [[Weighted Input]], and a [[Neural Network Bias]] shifts that value before an [[Activation Function]] calculates the output. This makes the unit a small parameterized computation that can be simulated in ordinary software; no literal artificial cell is required.

Kelleher's two-stage view distinguishes the weighted sum from the nonlinear activation applied afterward. A unit's output can be a final prediction or an intermediate learned feature passed to later units. He also shows that the bias can be represented as a weight on a constant input of one, making its calculation and training part of the same weighted-input structure.

19461.sourceSearchName: artin rees lemma artin rees lemma
19461.title: Artin-Rees Lemma
19461.heading: Artin-Rees Lemma
19461.content:
Let I be an ideal in a Noetherian ring, M a finitely generated module, and N a submodule. The Artin-Rees lemma says that for some k, IⁿM ∩ N = Iⁿ⁻ᵏ(IᵏM ∩ N) for all n ≥ k.

Thus the filtration induced on N eventually follows a fixed rule. The result controls intersections with ideal powers and supports [[Krull Intersection Theorem|Krull's intersection theorem]].

19464.title: Artificial Variable
19464.heading: Artificial Variable
19464.content:
An artificial variable is temporarily added to a constraint that lacks an obvious starting basic variable, especially an equality or greater-than-or-equal constraint.

It does not represent part of the original model and must be driven to zero. The [[Big M Method]] penalizes it in the objective, while the [[Two-Phase Simplex Method]] removes it through a separate feasibility phase.

19467.sourceSearchName: artificial neural network artificial neural network
19467.title: Artificial Neural Network
19467.heading: Artificial Neural Network
19467.content:
An artificial neural network is a parameterized network of simple computational units arranged in connected layers. Each unit combines weighted inputs, applies a nonlinear function, and passes its output onward.

Learning changes the connection weights so that the network maps inputs to useful outputs. Multiple layers form a [[Deep Neural Network]], while specialized connections support sequence and spatial processing.

Networks commonly arrange neurons into an input layer, one or more [[Hidden Layer|hidden layers]], and an output layer. A [[Dense Layer]] connects every unit to every neuron in the following layer, though other connection patterns can be chosen for different tasks. [[Forward Propagation]] carries activations toward the output, and [[Backpropagation]] sends parameter-adjustment information in the reverse direction during training.

Kelleher emphasizes that each processing neuron performs two steps: a weighted sum of incoming values and an [[Activation Function]] applied to that sum. The network's function is built by [[Neural Model Composition|composing]] those small transformations. For a fully connected layer, the sums can be evaluated together as [[Layer Matrix Computation|vector–matrix multiplication]], with nonlinear activations applied afterward. This mathematical regularity helps explain the suitability of GPU-style matrix hardware for repeated network runs.

19470.title: Artificial Moral Agent
19470.heading: Artificial Moral Agent
19470.content:
An artificial moral agent is a machine designed to select actions using moral rules, values, or learned evaluations. The design ambition ranges from systems that obey safety constraints to machines expected to resolve conflicts among values.

The central difficulty is that human ethics is not always a complete set of explicit rules. Moral judgment is also embodied, socially embedded, and sensitive to context. An artificial system may therefore display [[Functional Morality]] without possessing full [[Machine Moral Agency]]. Keeping that distinction clear prevents engineered compliance from being mistaken for moral understanding or responsibility.

19473.title: Artificial Intelligence
19473.heading: Artificial Intelligence
19473.content:
Artificial intelligence is the effort to build systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as recognizing speech, interpreting language, choosing actions, and learning from experience. The label covers both explicitly programmed methods such as an [[Expert System]] and data-driven methods such as [[Machine Learning]].

In a [[Virtual Assistant]], intelligence is distributed across specialized components rather than located in the conversational surface alone. Fluent language can make a system appear broadly intelligent even when its understanding and available actions remain narrow.

AI should also be understood as part of a sociotechnical system that includes data, infrastructure, organizations, users, and people affected without directly using it. Narrow systems can have broad ethical effects when institutions rely on their classifications or predictions. This is why [[AI Ethics]] addresses present design and deployment as well as speculative [[Artificial General Intelligence]].

19476.content:
Artificial general intelligence is the proposed ability of a machine to perform a wide range of intellectual tasks rather than succeed only within a narrow domain. It is often called strong AI and is contrasted with current systems optimized for tasks such as recognition, prediction, or game play.

General intelligence is central to forecasts of [[Superintelligence]] and a [[Technological Singularity]], but its feasibility and path of development remain uncertain. Ethical attention devoted to this possibility should not replace examination of existing narrow systems, whose limited intelligence can still have broad effects when embedded in social institutions.

19479.title: Articulatory Distance
19479.heading: Articulatory Distance
19479.content:
Articulatory distance is the gap between a player's intended action and the physical action required to express it through an interface. A direct, well-learned mapping has a shorter articulatory distance than an indirect or arbitrary one.

Reducing this distance lowers [[Cognitive Load]] in the input side of the [[User-System Loop]]. Its feedback-side counterpart is [[Semantic Distance]], the effort needed to interpret the system's response.

19494.title: ARPANET
19494.heading: ARPANET
19494.content:
ARPANET was a packet-switched research network funded by the United States Advanced Research Projects Agency. Its first computers were connected in 1969, linking university and government-supported computing centers.

The network demonstrated that heterogeneous computers could exchange data through shared protocols. Its technologies and research community became major ancestors of the Internet.

19497.sourceSearchName: arpanet protocol transition arpanet protocol transition
19497.title: ARPANET Protocol Transition
19497.heading: ARPANET Protocol Transition
19497.content:
ARPANET initially used a protocol designed for its limited network, then switched to TCP/IP in 1983 as scale and interconnection needs grew. The transition separated reliable message handling from movement of individual packets.

Changing a live network required participating hosts to adopt a coordinated standard. The successful migration created a foundation on which many different networks could interoperate.

19506.title: Arithmetic Progression
19506.heading: Arithmetic Progression
19506.content:
An arithmetic progression is a [[Sequence]] in which each term after the first is obtained by adding a constant [[Common Difference]]. The progression

$$2,7,12,17,\ldots$$

has common difference (5). Its values grow linearly with position, so the [[General Term of an Arithmetic Progression]] has the form (a_1+d(n-1)). Recognizing this form allows membership questions to become linear equations and long sums to be simplified through term pairing.

19509.title: Arithmetic Operation
19509.heading: Arithmetic Operation
19509.content:
An arithmetic operation combines or transforms numbers according to a defined rule. The elementary operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, exponentiation, and root extraction.

Some operations can be defined through earlier ones. Subtraction finds the value that must be added to recover a minuend, division finds the value that must be multiplied by a divisor, exponentiation abbreviates repeated multiplication, and a root reverses a power. Which results are allowed depends on the number system: natural numbers are closed under addition and multiplication but not under every subtraction or division.

19515.heading: Area Under the ROC Curve
19515.content:
Area under the ROC curve summarizes how often a classifier ranks a randomly chosen positive case above a randomly chosen negative case across thresholds. A value near one indicates strong separation, while one-half corresponds to chance ranking.

AUC does not specify an operating threshold or encode asymmetric error costs, so it complements rather than replaces decision-specific measures.

19518.title: Archimedes' Principle
19518.heading: Archimedes' Principle
19518.content: Archimedes' principle states that a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces. The force results from greater [[Hydrostatic Pressure]] on lower surfaces than on upper ones. Floating equilibrium occurs when buoyancy equals the object's weight.

Covariance, local linear models, or projected residuals can reveal this structure. The added flexibility increases estimation cost and makes solutions harder to summarize because relevance is expressed through combinations of features.

19524.title: Arbitrage
19524.heading: Arbitrage
19524.content:
Arbitrage is buying a resource in one place and selling it elsewhere for a higher price. It can create legitimate trading play when distance, time, risk, or limited capacity makes the difference costly to exploit.

An uncontrolled repeatable arbitrage loop creates currency from price mismatches and can rapidly destabilize a [[Game Economy]]. Designers must evaluate every conversion path and use [[Price Boundary|price boundaries]] or other constraints to prevent runaway gain.

19527.title: AR Stage
19527.heading: AR Stage
19527.content:
An AR stage is the spatial and situational setting in which authored actors and interactions operate. It includes relevant physical geometry, coordinate frames, anchors, display conditions, and the locations where events may occur.

Unlike a wholly virtual scene, the stage must accommodate an environment the system does not completely control. Setup and calibration connect the authored representation to the particular physical place where it is performed.

19539.content:
AR authoring defines the content, semantics, behavior, and interaction of an augmented-reality experience. It goes beyond producing individual models by arranging actors, stages, story, interactions, and setup into an application the user can experience.

An authoring system should expose real-world relationships without requiring every creator to implement tracking and rendering infrastructure. Hardware abstraction and reusable workflows keep content decisions separate from changing device details.

Rapid iteration matters because spatial relationships are difficult to judge outside the target environment. Previewing the experience through its intended display reveals registration, scale, occlusion, and interaction problems early.

19554.title: AR Actor
19554.heading: AR Actor
19554.content:
An AR actor is a real or virtual entity that participates in an authored augmented experience. An actor has an identity and may carry geometry, appearance, state, behavior, or relationships to other actors and physical anchors.

Treating both real and virtual entities as actors lets the author define interactions across the real-virtual boundary. A tracked physical object can therefore trigger or constrain behavior just as a generated character can.

19557.title: Apriori Algorithm
19557.heading: Apriori Algorithm
19557.content:
Apriori discovers frequent itemsets level by level. It finds frequent one-item sets, joins the frequent sets of length k minus one to form length-k candidates, scans the transactions for support, and repeats until no candidates qualify.

The algorithm relies on downward closure to prune any candidate containing an infrequent subset before expensive counting.

19559.title: Approximation Complex

19560.title: Approximation Complex
19560.heading: Approximation Complex
19560.content:
An approximation complex is built from cycles, boundaries, or homology of a [[Koszul Complex]] tensored with a symmetric algebra. It reorganizes syzygy information into a graded complex.

Its zeroth homology can recover the symmetric algebra of an ideal or of its conormal module. Acyclicity conditions connect linear-type ideals, Rees algebras, and determinant formulas used in implicitization.

19563.title: Approximation Algorithm
19563.heading: Approximation Algorithm
19563.content:
An approximation algorithm seeks a solution that may not be optimal but is acceptably close to the optimum. It is useful when an exact solution exists mathematically yet the required [[Computational Complexity]] makes exact search impractical.

The tradeoff is deliberate rather than accidental. For an [[Intractable Problem]] such as the [[Traveling Salesman Problem]], a near-optimal route found in reasonable time can be more useful than an exact method that cannot finish on realistic input.

19566.title: Approximate Search
19566.heading: Approximate Search
19566.content:
Approximate search looks for items similar enough to a target rather than requiring an exact match. The search therefore needs a way to measure or rank similarity and a rule for deciding which candidates are acceptable.

A spellchecker illustrates the distinction: an unrecognized spelling may not occur in its dictionary, so it searches for nearby words that could have been intended. This changes both the meaning of success and the work required from a [[Search Algorithm]].

19569.title: Application Virtualization
19569.heading: Application Virtualization
19569.content:
Application virtualization hosts an application centrally and delivers access to many users without requiring the full application to be installed and managed on every client. Users interact through a browser, mobile client, or a remote presentation of the hosted application.

Central hosting can share application costs and let comparatively modest devices use demanding software. If application data is also stored remotely, a user becomes less dependent on one physical device or location.

19572.sourceSearchName: approximate bayesian inference approximate bayesian inference
19572.title: Approximate Bayesian Inference
19572.heading: Approximate Bayesian Inference
19572.content:
Approximate Bayesian inference replaces an intractable exact calculation with a controlled estimate of the requested distribution or statistic. Sampling and optimization are common ways to trade precision for feasible computation.

The approximation should be interpreted as part of the answer, not as a hidden implementation detail. Its error depends on the model, proposal mechanism, sample count, convergence, and the particular question being asked.

An application speedup profile records how execution time changes as more processors are assigned. Perfectly parallel work would finish in inverse proportion to processor count, but sequential sections, communication, and synchronization create diminishing returns.

Schedulers use the measured profile to avoid giving cores to an application that cannot use them effectively.

19584.heading: Application Service
19584.content: An application service exposes operations that coordinate domain use cases without owning the business rules. It accepts [[Application Command]]s or explicit parameters, loads an [[Aggregate]] through the [[Repository Pattern]], calls the aggregate's behavior, and commits changes. It can group related operations behind one dependency where separate [[Command Handler]]s would be cumbersome. The service remains thin when decisions about validity and state transitions stay inside the domain model.

The application security layer protects the programs through which users and systems process data. It includes secure design, input handling, identity and permission checks, testing, and maintenance throughout the [[Secure Software Development Lifecycle]].

Application weaknesses may expose data even when networks and hosts are well defended. [[Security Code Review]], [[Security Architecture Analysis]], and [[Penetration Testing]] examine different aspects of this layer before and after deployment.

19590.heading: Application Query
19590.content: An application query expresses a request for information without changing domain state. It names the user's retrieval intent and returns a purpose-specific [[Read Model]]. Unlike an [[Application Command]], it does not need to load an aggregate or enforce state-transition invariants. A query can access storage through an efficient read path, including joins across aggregate data, while still using the [[Ubiquitous Language]] of the decision or screen it supports.

19593.content:
An application pack is a group of parallel tasks scheduled to run concurrently on a fixed pool of processors. The pack finishes when its slowest member finishes, so processor assignments should reduce the maximum execution time rather than optimize each task independently.

Co-scheduling can partition a workload into several packs and execute those packs in sequence.

19596.content: The application layer coordinates a use case around an isolated [[Domain Model]]. It receives a [[Public API Contract]] or message, obtains the required aggregate or services, invokes domain behavior, and persists the resulting changes. It can implement infrastructure-facing interfaces declared by the domain, but it should not reimplement [[Entity Invariant]]s. The layer is an outer boundary: it translates between delivery mechanisms and the domain while keeping business decisions in domain objects.

19599.heading: Application Configuration
19599.content:
Application configuration separates adjustable settings from the code that consumes them. In an ASP.NET Core project, root files such as `Program.cs`, `Startup.cs`, and `appsettings.json` coordinate hosting, services, middleware, compilation, and publication behavior.

Environment-specific files can override general values for a [[Development Environment]], [[Staging Environment]], or [[Production Environment]]. Configuration values may be read by key or bound to typed classes so the rest of the application uses a defined model.

19602.title: Application Command
19602.heading: Application Command
19602.content: An application command is a message that asks the system to perform an action that may change state. It captures [[Command Intent]] in a serializable form, such as creating an item or changing its price, without containing the business behavior itself. A [[Command Handler]] or [[Application Service]] converts command values into domain types and invokes an [[Aggregate]]. Successful processing can produce one or more [[Domain Event]]s; rejection leaves the model in a valid state.

19605.content:
Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007 as a touch-centered convergence of phone, networked computer, media player, camera, and later an application platform. Its interface placed direct manipulation ahead of physical keys.

The product triggered rapid smartphone adoption and a large software ecosystem. Its impact came from coordinated hardware, software, networking, and design rather than a single new component.

19608.heading: Apple iPad
19608.content:
The iPad extended Apple’s touch interface and mobile operating environment to a larger tablet display. It combined Wi-Fi or cellular networking with a form suited to reading, media, browsing, and direct manipulation.

Tablet computers had existed earlier, but the iPad achieved broad adoption through an established application ecosystem and coherent user experience. It illustrates how timing and integration can matter more than being first.

19611.title: Apple II
19611.heading: Apple II
19611.content:
The Apple II combined a capable personal computer with attractive packaging, color graphics, expansion slots, and professional marketing. Its design made computing approachable beyond the kit-building hobbyist community.

Applications such as VisiCalc gave the machine practical business value, while games and graphics broadened consumer appeal. The product established Apple as a major personal-computer company.

19614.title: Apple I
19614.heading: Apple I
19614.content:
The Apple I was Steve Wozniak’s 6502-based personal computer design, sold initially as an assembled circuit board. Users supplied the case, power supply, keyboard, and display.

Its elegant economy emerged from close knowledge of available components. The machine led Wozniak and Steve Jobs to found Apple and develop a more complete consumer system.

This protects historical traceability, but consumers must interpret the complete sequence or an up-to-date projection to obtain the effective current value.

19620.heading: Appearance Modeling
19620.content:
Appearance modeling records how a physical or virtual surface should look when rendered. Color, texture, reflectance, transparency, and illumination response may be sampled from the scene or assigned through authoring controls.

Geometry alone can support registration and occlusion, but a convincing reconstruction also needs appearance that changes plausibly with viewpoint and light. The required detail depends on whether the model is used for measurement, visualization, or photometric composition.

Game artificial intelligence is judged by whether behavior appears purposeful, responsive, and suitable for play rather than by whether it reproduces general human intelligence. A simpler system can be more effective when it is predictable enough to learn yet varied enough to remain believable.

Pathfinding, behavior states, and planning therefore serve the designed experience. Their computation must fit within the time available for a frame and may deliberately expose patterns the player can understand.

19629.heading: API Token Validation
19629.content:
API token validation checks a presented access token before a protected controller action runs. The API is configured with an authentication scheme, the IdentityServer authority, and the resource name it expects the token to represent.

An authorization attribute then marks the controller or operation as protected. The client sets a bearer token on its HTTP calls, and requests without an acceptable token are rejected before business logic is trusted to execute.

19632.title: API Request Model
19632.heading: API Request Model
19632.content:
An API request model defines the fields accepted by one HTTP operation. It gives model binding and validation a transport-specific target instead of accepting a persistence entity as an unrestricted request body.

A focused request model makes writable fields explicit and can carry validation rules suited to that operation. Separate models may be appropriate when create and update requests have different requirements.

19635.title: API Controller
19635.heading: API Controller
19635.content:
An API controller is an ASP.NET Core class whose actions expose application behavior over HTTP. Routing selects the controller and action, model binding constructs inputs, and the returned action result becomes the HTTP response.

The controller should coordinate the transport boundary rather than own persistence details. It validates the request, calls an injected repository or service, and translates the outcome into an appropriate response.

19638.title: Apache Tez
19638.heading: Apache Tez
19638.content:
Apache Tez is a Hadoop execution framework that represents a job as a directed acyclic graph of processing stages rather than a fixed sequence of separate MapReduce jobs. It can avoid unnecessary materialization and coordinate a more efficient dataflow.

Query systems can compile higher-level plans into Tez graphs while YARN supplies the cluster resources.

19641.title: Aperture
19641.heading: Aperture
19641.content:
Aperture is the adjustable opening that controls how much light passes through a camera lens. A wider opening admits more light, while a narrower opening admits less and therefore requires compensation through shutter time, sensitivity, or scene illumination.

Aperture also influences [[Depth of Field]]. This makes it forensically useful: a recorded f-number can be compared with how quickly objects before and behind the focus distance become blurred, provided the analyst also considers focal length and subject distance.

19644.title: Apache Pig
19644.heading: Apache Pig
19644.content:
Apache Pig is a high-level dataflow system for transforming large collections of semi-structured data in Hadoop-compatible storage. Its compiler turns [[Pig Latin]] operations into ordered MapReduce jobs and submits them for parallel execution.

Pig is suited to extract-transform-load pipelines, log processing, and custom analytics. It hides much of the job-level code while allowing [[User-Defined Function|user-defined functions]] for specialized transformations.

19647.title: Apache Hive
19647.heading: Apache Hive
19647.content:
Apache Hive is a distributed data-warehouse system for large structured datasets stored through the Hadoop ecosystem. It uses [[HiveQL]] and a metastore containing schemas and statistics to compile queries into parallel jobs.

The catalog enables operations such as column and partition pruning, join planning, and indexed access. Hive favors structured, high-latency analytical queries rather than procedural transformation of unstructured records.

19650.title: Apache Harp
19650.heading: Apache Harp
19650.content:
Apache Harp is presented as a Hadoop plug-in that adds long-running map workers and [[Collective Communication]] for iterative computations. Its MapCollective interface lets a program retain processes and reusable data across repeated rounds.

The book integrates Harp with Pig so high-level scripts can run K-means and PageRank without restarting a complete Hadoop job for every iteration. The resulting workflow exchanges partial updates in memory.

19653.title: Apache Hadoop
19653.heading: Apache Hadoop
19653.content:
Apache Hadoop provides distributed storage, resource management, and MapReduce execution for data spread across a cluster. High-level systems can compile their scripts into Hadoop jobs instead of requiring users to implement every parallel task directly.

Its disk-oriented job boundaries scale one-pass processing but add startup, cleanup, and repeated-read costs to iterative analytics. Extensions can preserve data and worker processes across iterations.

19656.heading: Anticipating Software Breakdowns
19656.content:
Anticipating software breakdowns means imagining failures and harmful consequences before they occur. Designers examine user mistakes, attacks, organizational disruption, lost data, and changes in the surrounding environment.

Useful responses include undo, continuous backup, safe defaults, graceful degradation, and post-delivery repair. The practice treats recovery and care as parts of the product rather than exceptions left to users.

19659.heading: Antimonotone Constraint
19659.content:
An antimonotone constraint has the property that if an itemset violates it, every superset also violates it. This permits an entire branch of the search lattice to be pruned as soon as one failing pattern is found.

Minimum support is the standard example: adding items cannot increase the number of transactions containing the set.

19662.heading: Anthropocentrism in AI Ethics
19662.content:
Anthropocentrism in AI ethics places human beings and human interests at the center of moral evaluation. It can protect human dignity against systems that prioritize efficiency, but it may also assume that resemblance to humans is the main route to intelligence, agency, or moral worth.

The assumption affects both machines and the environment. It can exclude unfamiliar artificial beings from consideration and neglect the effects of AI on animals, ecosystems, and future conditions for life. [[Posthumanism]] challenges this hierarchy, while [[Human-Centered AI]] attempts to retain protection for human agency within practical governance.

19665.title: Anisotropic Filtering
19665.heading: Anisotropic Filtering
19665.content:
Anisotropic filtering improves texture sampling when a surface is viewed at an oblique angle and its footprint is stretched differently along two directions. It samples a non-square region instead of relying only on one isotropic mip level.

The method preserves distant angled detail that otherwise becomes overly blurred. Higher anisotropy levels use more texture samples and therefore trade additional work for improved quality.

A pose may come directly from a keyframe or be interpolated between neighboring samples in an [[Animation Clip]]. Its global transforms combine with inverse bind matrices to form the palette used for vertex skinning.

19683.heading: Animated Water from Displacement Maps
19683.content: Still water in an image can be made to move by displacing a masked copy of the plate with an animated grayscale map. The book constructs wave-like noise with blur, directional blur, contrast adjustment, and scaling to match the pictured ripple pattern. The map drifts slowly in the apparent wave direction; its contrast or the displacement control governs strength. A roto limits the displaced copy to water, while the original still plate remains intact underneath. Large movement breaks the illusion, so subtlety is part of the method.

19686.title: Animation Clip
19686.heading: Animation Clip
19686.content:
An animation clip stores a named sequence of skeletal poses over a duration and sampling rate. Playback converts elapsed time into neighboring frame indices and a fractional interpolation amount.

Looping wraps time back into the clip's duration, while one-shot playback clamps or transitions when the end is reached. The clip supplies local bone transforms rather than final skinned vertex positions.

19689.heading: Animated Proportional Symbols
19689.content: Animated proportional symbols keep point locations fixed while changing symbol radius, color, or both through time. The source animates station circles whose size encodes measured value and whose color distinguishes weekdays from weekends. Stable identities help viewers follow each location, while missing values can be mapped to zero size. A [[Animation Progress Bar|time reference]] is needed because repeated motion alone does not reveal the current date.

19692.title: Animated Map
19692.heading: Animated Map
19692.content: An animated map presents successive spatial states as frames so movement and change can be perceived over time. Effectiveness depends on similarity between consecutive frames: smooth enough transitions support object continuity, while abrupt unrelated frames are difficult to integrate into one story. Stable extent, color scale, and geographic context are essential. A [[Static Small-Multiple Complement]] preserves positions that transient motion makes hard to compare.

19698.title: Angular

Angular is a client-side framework for building reactive, cross-platform web applications for desktop and mobile browsers. It combines a component-based and modular application structure with templates, routing, dependency injection, forms, HTTP communication, and testing support.

Angular source is commonly written in [[TypeScript]] and compiled into JavaScript understood by browsers. In a full-stack application it supplies the client while [[ASP.NET Core]] exposes server-side endpoints and persistence operations.

19701.title: Animal-Derived Serum
19701.heading: Animal-Derived Serum
19701.content:
Animal-derived serum is a blood fraction added to culture medium because it contains proteins, attachment factors, hormones, and growth signals that support many cell types. Its complex composition makes it broadly useful.

Serum varies between donor animals and production batches, complicates reproducibility, and maintains reliance on animals, which motivates [[Serum-Free Medium]].

19704.title: Angular Velocity
19704.heading: Angular Velocity
19704.content: Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement, $\omega=d\theta/dt$. For circular motion at radius $r$, tangential speed is $v=r\omega$. Its vector direction lies along the rotation axis according to the right-hand rule. Constant angular velocity still gives changing linear velocity because the direction of motion continually turns.

19707.title: Angular Workspace
19707.heading: Angular Workspace
19707.content:
An Angular workspace is the project-level structure containing client source, build configuration, package metadata, TypeScript settings, and testing configuration. Files such as `angular.json`, `package.json`, and `tsconfig.json` govern different parts of that toolchain.

Within a combined ASP.NET Core template, the workspace lives under the client application folder, while its compiled static output is served through the back-end project.

19710.title: Angular TestBed
19710.heading: Angular TestBed
19710.content:
Angular TestBed configures a testing module for components and services. It declares the units under test, supplies imported capabilities and providers, compiles components, and creates fixtures.

TestBed can replace a production [[Angular Service]] with a [[Test Double]]. The test then accesses the component and rendered template through the created [[Test Fixture]].
